$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{d}\,c & =|\,c\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡({60}^{∘}) \\  & =16\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $d:$

$$
u=\frac{d}{|\,d\,|}=\frac{d}{4}=\frac{1}{4}d
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{d}\,c & ={\text{comp}}_{d}\,c\cdot u \\  & =8\cdot \frac{1}{4}d \\  & =2d\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0478e591-82c4-56f2-9e83-eb51b18b93e3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0478e591-82c4-56f2-9e83-eb51b18b93e3" :answer-field/id #uuid "0478e591-82c4-56f2-9e83-eb51b18b93e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d281791a-6600-51ff-a350-02e5807be308" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a927a06b-c1ab-5420-bff4-edf63dc12fe1" "answer-d281791a-6600-51ff-a350-02e5807be308" "answer-8ab5504e-47f2-5106-b694-7a718d03210a" "answer-d2a38c14-4542-5cbc-a049-1870202ed396" "answer-4898f0e7-39a5-5f06-8e56-8f5aafed918a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a927a06b-c1ab-5420-bff4-edf63dc12fe1" :answer/id #uuid "a927a06b-c1ab-5420-bff4-edf63dc12fe1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16d" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d281791a-6600-51ff-a350-02e5807be308" :answer/id #uuid "d281791a-6600-51ff-a350-02e5807be308" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2d" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ab5504e-47f2-5106-b694-7a718d03210a" :answer/id #uuid "8ab5504e-47f2-5106-b694-7a718d03210a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4d" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2a38c14-4542-5cbc-a049-1870202ed396" :answer/id #uuid "d2a38c14-4542-5cbc-a049-1870202ed396" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8d" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4898f0e7-39a5-5f06-8e56-8f5aafed918a" :answer/id #uuid "4898f0e7-39a5-5f06-8e56-8f5aafed918a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "d" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106480 :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,c\,|=12$, $|\,d\,|=6$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Find the vector projection of $d$ onto $c$ in terms of the vector $c.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{c}\,d & =|\,d\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $c:$

$$
u=\frac{c}{|\,c\,|}=\frac{c}{12}=\frac{1}{12}c
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{c}\,d & ={\text{comp}}_{c}\,d\cdot u \\  & =(-3)\cdot \frac{1}{12}c \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}c\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105028 :answer-field/correct 17592186105031 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-24948042-4caf-54ad-85ae-20d1f75949ff" :question/id #uuid "24948042-4caf-54ad-85ae-20d1f75949ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-316438" :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,x\,|=9$, $|\,y\,|=6$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\pi .$ Find the vector projection of $x$ onto $y$ in terms of the vector $y.$

${\text{proj}}_{y}\,x=$
{{field-1}}
$y$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{y}\,x & =|\,x\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =9\cdot (-1) \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $y:$

$$
u=\frac{y}{|\,y\,|}=\frac{y}{6}=\frac{1}{6}y
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{y}\,x & ={\text{comp}}_{y}\,x\cdot u \\  & =-9\cdot \frac{1}{6}y \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\,y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-42723228-7b18-5999-8f79-63b014252842"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-42723228-7b18-5999-8f79-63b014252842" :answer-field/id #uuid "42723228-7b18-5999-8f79-63b014252842" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-0ae82f23-3f33-55f8-b143-c4e2aa44358a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0ae82f23-3f33-55f8-b143-c4e2aa44358a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0ae82f23-3f33-55f8-b143-c4e2aa44358a" :answer/id #uuid "0ae82f23-3f33-55f8-b143-c4e2aa44358a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8e5a64ce-22c5-5e8c-997a-c2e3826ce849" :question/id #uuid "8e5a64ce-22c5-5e8c-997a-c2e3826ce849" :question/math-academy-id "q-275227" :question/problem "Suppose that $|\,a\,|=16$, $|\,b\,|=2$ and that the angle between the vectors is $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Find the vector projection of $a$ onto $b$ in terms of the vector $b.$

$b$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$

$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $b:$

$$
u=\frac{b}{|\,b\,|}=\frac{b}{2}=\frac{1}{2}b
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{1}{2}b \\  & =-4\,b.\end{aligned}

$$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107168 :tutorial/content "Notice that if two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, then by projecting $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$), we obtain the zero vector.

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

*If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105967 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

["question-25a56934-09b0-592a-b002-4f360029a2ea" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =0\cdot 11+4\cdot x+3\cdot 2 \\  & =4x+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 4x+6 & =0 \\ 4x & =-6 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-25a56934-09b0-592a-b002-4f360029a2ea" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-454a546d-b2cd-5e75-93bf-898cf6aab9d8" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-fc72b4b3-1726-5899-88e5-9bd9e302a6a9"] [17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

that the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}.$ Find the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ in terms of the vector $\mathbf{b}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the scalar projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6}) \\  & =8\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4} \mathbf{b}
$$

Finally, we compute the vector projection as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-4\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{1}{4}b \\  & =-\sqrt{3}b\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186106111 :question/id #uuid "923b55ee-6062-5c44-a28a-51ce2a7ca4a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-19219"} {:db/id 17592186106480 :question/id #uuid "e48c0a41-451d-5386-8afe-32a1dfe30bdb" :question/math-academy-id "q-71836" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9c46506b-71f4-5dd4-8073-f478001468d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4c" :db/id 17592186105029} {:answer/id #uuid "aa28895b-01c4-5a6a-8497-a8805ff0c18e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}c" :db/id 17592186105030} {:answer/id #uuid "0bd413b9-0ccc-5243-898a-0e04480488f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}c" :db/id 17592186105031} {:answer/id #uuid "371bec7c-71dd-546e-8bff-407c6e758672" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{4}c" :db/id 17592186105032} {:answer/id #uuid "7c124655-5867-56b0-ab0d-79de478b24e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-4c" :db/id 17592186105033}] :answer-field/id #uuid "295493ed-d510-566e-997d-2641481e7989" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186105028}] :question/problem "Suppose that $\mid c|= 12$, $\mid d|= 6$ and that the angle between the vectors is $θ = \frac{2π}{3}$. projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =1\cdot 1+3\cdot (-2)+2\cdot x \\  & =2x-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 2x-5 & =0 \\ 2x & =5 \\ x & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186292822 :question/id #uuid "42205966-0418-52d2-acb8-9c430cb90d52" :question/math-academy-id "q-275234"} {:db/id 17592186292823 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1295} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "26031206-512a-5b41-90d5-299987889655" :step/math-academy-id 121755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106650}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "146819e4-ecad-5e47-8884-a05b59624d07" :step/math-academy-id 121763} {:db/id 17592186106567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107168 :tutorial/content "Notice that if two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, then by projecting $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$), we obtain the zero vector.

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

> *If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "ec38d18e-577a-5ebc-8349-60991ef75b80" :step/math-academy-id 121766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106566}} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}}] :activity/title "Calculating a Vector Projection" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105967} {:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" :step/math-academy-id 121759 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106565}} {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

> *If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
